messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Hale is a 42-year-old married ship captain of mixed North American heritage who presented for psychological assessment following a referral from his maritime employer after colleagues raised concerns about his erratic decision-making on the water. He carries a PCL-5 score of 56, consistent with significant post-traumatic stress, and his presentation is best understood against the backdrop of a catastrophic industrial explosion he survived three years ago at a commercial port facility.

Marcus had been overseeing a cargo transfer operation when a pressurised tank on an adjacent vessel detonated without warning. The blast wave threw him across the deck; he watched crew members he had commanded for years disappear into smoke and fire. Port security personnel — uniformed officers he did not recognise — arrived in the chaos and, in his account, gave contradictory orders that delayed the evacuation and may have cost lives. No formal inquiry ever assigned individual responsibility to those officers or to the facility operators whose maintenance failures precipitated the explosion. Marcus left the scene physically intact but carrying the conviction that the people who should have protected his crew had failed them, and that no one had been made to answer for it.

That conviction — that those responsible faced no consequences and that other people fundamentally cannot be relied upon — became the lens through which Marcus now reads the world, and it has amplified the threat he perceives in nearly every environment. He has come to believe that because institutions failed once without penalty, they will fail again, and that the only variable he can control is his own vigilance. In any room he enters, Marcus scans for dangerous individuals and selects his seat based on sightlines and proximity to exits; at sea or ashore, he cannot fall asleep without first satisfying himself that no threat is approaching, a process that can take hours. The appraisal that others are unreliable feeds directly into a sustained sense that danger is always present and unguarded against.

The triggers that return him most forcefully to the explosion are precisely those that were present in those minutes on the deck: the sudden concussive sound of anything that bangs or detonates nearby, the sight of military or police uniforms, and the physical act of objects being thrown, which replicates the sensation of being hurled by the blast. Because Marcus now appraises the world as perpetually unsafe and staffed by people who cannot be trusted, these sensory cues carry a weight far beyond their objective content — the sight of a uniformed harbour officer is not merely uncomfortable but registers as evidence that the conditions for catastrophe are reassembling. His body responds accordingly, and the intrusive re-experiencing that follows confirms, in his mind, that the danger was and remains real.

To manage this, Marcus has developed a set of strategies that initially provided relief but have steadily eroded his functioning. He has quietly relinquished supervisory responsibilities on complex docking manoeuvres, delegating decisions that are properly his so as to avoid the concentrated exposure to noise, uniforms, and the unpredictability of other people that such operations involve. He has also taken to gambling — first at online platforms, then at a casino two towns from his home — finding that the focused, rule-bound tension of cards temporarily displaces the ambient hypervigilance that otherwise dominates his waking hours. His wife has noticed both the absences and the financial withdrawals but does not know their source. Over time, however, stepping back from his professional duties has deepened Marcus's sense that he is no longer capable, and the gambling, which began as distraction, has become a source of shame that reinforces his belief that he cannot be relied upon — that the same unreliability he attributes to others has now colonised him. That shame feeds back into the threat monitoring: if he cannot trust himself, he must be even more vigilant externally.

He avoids unfamiliar ports and anchorages entirely, unwilling to enter environments whose danger he cannot pre-calculate. He has not told his wife the full account of the explosion, partly because he is certain that revisiting it in any sustained way will overwhelm him beyond recovery. What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a near-miss incident in which his inattention during a routine harbour approach — his attention consumed by scanning the dock for threats — almost resulted in a collision. He is most afraid that he is becoming the kind of captain who gets people killed. What he most hopes is that someone can explain why he cannot simply decide to stop.
